**Apple of Discord, "To the Fairest"**
Eris, the goddess of discord, was not invited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, so she threw in a golden apple inscribed "To the Fairest." Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each claimed it, and the dispute set off the chain of events that led to the Trojan War.

**Judgment of Paris**
Zeus had the Trojan prince Paris decide which goddess deserved the apple. Paris gave it to Aphrodite, who had promised him the most beautiful woman in the world, Helen of Sparta, and his abduction of her started the Trojan War.

**Hippomenes (Melanion) and Atalanta's footrace**
The huntress Atalanta would only marry a man who could beat her in a footrace, and losers were killed. Aphrodite gave Hippomenes (called Melanion in some versions) three golden apples, which he dropped during the race; Atalanta stopped to pick them up, so he won and married her.

**Idunn and the apples of youth**
In Norse myth, the goddess Idunn keeps a box (eski) of apples that the gods eat to stay young. Without them, the Aesir begin to age and grow gray.

**Thiazi's kidnapping of Idunn**
The giant Thiazi, in the form of an eagle, captured Loki and forced him to lure Idunn and her apples out of Asgard. When the gods started aging, they made Loki get her back, so he borrowed Freyja's falcon form, turned Idunn into a nut and flew her home, and the gods killed Thiazi as he chased them.

**Heracles' eleventh labor**
King Eurystheus ordered Heracles to bring back golden apples from the Garden of the Hesperides. On the way he caught the sea god Nereus to make him reveal where the garden was, and survived King Busiris of Egypt, who tried to sacrifice him.

**Atlas fetches the apples**
In one version of the eleventh labor, Heracles held up the sky while Atlas, father of the Hesperides, collected the apples. When Atlas wanted to leave Heracles holding the sky forever, Heracles asked him to take it back for a moment to adjust his cloak, then walked off with the apples.

**Garden of the Hesperides**
The garden at the western edge of the world where the golden apples grew. It was tended by the Hesperides, nymphs of the evening often called the daughters of Atlas.

**Ladon**
The hundred-headed dragon that never slept and coiled around the golden apple tree in the Garden of the Hesperides. In some versions Heracles killed Ladon to take the apples, and Hera placed it in the sky as the constellation Draco.

**Gaia's wedding gift to Hera**
The golden apple tree first came from Gaia, who gave it to Hera (or to Zeus and Hera) as a wedding present. Hera planted it in the Garden of the Hesperides, and the tree was sacred to her.

**The Firebird and Prince Ivan**
In the Russian fairy tale, the Firebird keeps stealing golden apples from the tsar's orchard at night. Prince Ivan (Ivan Tsarevich) sets out to catch it, beginning his adventures with the gray wolf.

**Manannan mac Lir's Silver Bough**
In Irish myth, the sea god Manannan mac Lir gave King Cormac mac Airt a silver branch hung with three golden apples. When shaken, it played music so sweet that it put listeners, even the sick and wounded, to sleep.

**Volsung's conception**
In the Volsunga saga, King Rerir and his wife could not have a child. Frigg (through Odin) sent them an apple, carried by the giantess Hljod in the form of a crow, and after eating it the queen conceived the hero Volsung.

**Skirnir's wooing of Gerd**
In the Eddic poem Skirnismal, Freyr's servant Skirnir offers the giantess Gerd eleven golden apples and the ring Draupnir to persuade her to marry Freyr. When she refuses the gifts, he threatens her with curses until she agrees.

**Golden apples in Slavic and Balkan folklore**
Golden apples appear across Eastern European tales: thieving peahens steal them in a Bulgarian tale, zmeu dragons take them in Romanian legend, and in some Slavic myths the thunder god Perun throws golden apples as balls of lightning.
